import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm, t as scipy_t, skewnorm

# ---- EDITABLE STRATEGY PARAMETERS ----
strategies = [
    dict(
        title='4th-Down Aggression',
        bucket='analytics / game_management',
        family='skew_normal',
        xi=0.72, omega=0.82, alpha=2.0,
        most_plausible=1.2
    ),
    dict(
        title='Early-Down Pass Rate',
        bucket='analytics / offensive',
        family='skew_normal',
        xi=0.44, omega=0.82, alpha=1.8,
        most_plausible=0.9
    ),
    dict(
        title='Reduce Blitz on Passing Downs',
        bucket='analytics / defensive',
        family='normal',
        mu=0.75, sigma=0.995,
        most_plausible=0.75
    ),
    dict(
        title='Tactical Timeout for Momentum',
        bucket='intuition / game_management',
        family='student_t',
        nu=5, mu=0.30, sigma=0.603,
        most_plausible=0.30
    ),
    dict(
        title='No-Huddle Tempo Bursts',
        bucket='intuition / offensive',
        family='skew_normal',
        xi=0.34, omega=1.01, alpha=2.0,
        most_plausible=0.9
    ),
    dict(
        title='Aggressive DL Rotation',
        bucket='intuition / defensive',
        family='skew_normal',
        xi=0.15, omega=0.80, alpha=1.5,
        most_plausible=0.55
    ),
]
# ---- END EDITABLE SECTION ----


def make_dist(s):
    if s['family'] == 'normal':
        return norm(loc=s['mu'], scale=s['sigma'])
    elif s['family'] == 'student_t':
        return scipy_t(df=s['nu'], loc=s['mu'], scale=s['sigma'])
    else:
        return skewnorm(a=s['alpha'], loc=s['xi'], scale=s['omega'])


def param_string(s):
    if s['family'] == 'normal':
        return 'normal(mu=%.4f, sigma=%.4f)' % (s['mu'], s['sigma'])
    elif s['family'] == 'student_t':
        return 'student_t(nu=%d, mu=%.4f, sigma=%.4f)' % (s['nu'], s['mu'], s['sigma'])
    else:
        return 'skew_normal(xi=%.4f, omega=%.4f, alpha=%.4f)' % (s['xi'], s['omega'], s['alpha'])


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 9))
axes = axes.flatten()

for strat, ax in zip(strategies, axes):
    dist = make_dist(strat)
    mp = strat['most_plausible']

    lo = dist.ppf(0.025)
    hi = dist.ppf(0.975)

    x_min = dist.ppf(0.0005)
    x_max = dist.ppf(0.9995)
    x = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 900)
    y = dist.pdf(x)

    ax.plot(x, y, color='steelblue', linewidth=2.0, zorder=3)

    mask = (x >= lo) & (x <= hi)
    ax.fill_between(x[mask], y[mask], alpha=0.28, color='steelblue', zorder=2,
                    label='95%% CI (from ppf): [%.2f, %.2f]' % (lo, hi))

    ax.axvline(mp, color='crimson', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.8, zorder=4,
               label='Most plausible: %.2f' % mp)

    ax.set_xlabel('Change in own scoring margin (points)', fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylabel('Density', fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title('%s\n[%s]' % (strat['title'], strat['bucket']), fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc='upper right')
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.axvline(0, color='grey', linewidth=0.6, linestyle=':', zorder=1)

    pstr = param_string(strat)
    print('Strategy : %s' % strat['title'])
    print('  Bucket  : %s' % strat['bucket'])
    print('  Family  : %s' % pstr)
    print('  95%% interval from dist.ppf : [%.4f, %.4f]' % (lo, hi))
    print('  Most plausible (stated)     :  %.4f' % mp)
    print()

plt.suptitle('NFL Strategy Priors: Change in Expected Scoring Margin (points)',
             fontsize=11, fontweight='bold', y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=1.2 lies inside interval_95=[-0.6, 2.7]. skew_normal has full real support, covering signed scoring-margin values. Mode estimate uses approximate mode_z for alpha=2; small numerical discrepancy expected and visible in plot.

distribution_family.justification: The analytics strongly point to positive expected value, placing more prior mass on the upside, but failed conversions, turnovers on downs, and opponent field position recoveries create a meaningful left tail that prevents full confidence in a large positive effect.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically. For alpha=2.0: delta=2/sqrt(5)≈0.894; mode_z (standard skew-normal)≈0.56. Mode≈xi+omega*mode_z=0.72+0.82*0.56≈1.18≈1.2. Standard skew_normal(alpha=2) has ppf(0.025)≈-1.60 and ppf(0.975)≈2.37; scaled: ppf(0.025)≈0.72+0.82*(-1.60)≈-0.59 and ppf(0.975)≈0.72+0.82*2.37≈2.66. Stated interval [-0.6, 2.7] reflects these approximate values. Parameters are approximate; the plot script will show exact ppf values from scipy.

strategies.rationale: Win-probability and expected-points models consistently show league-wide punt rates on 4th-and-short in opponent territory exceed the analytically optimal rate by roughly 30–40 percentage points. Converting extends possessions and denies the opponent a full-field drive; even failed attempts leave the opponent pinned in their own half on average. Every incremental conversion at these rates is worth positive expected points.
strategies.recommendation: On 4th-and-1 or 4th-and-2 anywhere inside the opponent's 40-yard line, default to going for it rather than punting or attempting a long field goal. Extend the rule to 4th-and-3 inside the opponent's 35 in neutral game states (score within one possession).
strategies.title: Aggressive 4th-Down Conversion

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=0.9 lies inside interval_95=[-0.9, 2.3]. skew_normal support is all reals. Parameters are numerically approximate; exact interval recoverable from plot's ppf shading.

distribution_family.justification: Analytics support is real but the realized effect is sensitive to roster composition (is the OL a true pass-protecting unit?), play-action interaction effects, and defensive adjustment over the course of a season, motivating a moderate left tail.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically. For alpha=1.8: mode_z≈0.55 (approximate). Mode≈xi+omega*mode_z=0.44+0.82*0.55≈0.895≈0.9. Standard skew_normal(alpha=1.8) has ppf(0.025)≈-1.65, ppf(0.975)≈2.30; scaled: ppf(0.025)≈0.44+0.82*(-1.65)≈-0.91 and ppf(0.975)≈0.44+0.82*2.30≈2.33. Stated interval [-0.9, 2.3] matches.

strategies.rationale: Expected Points Added per play on early downs shows a persistent gap across multi-season samples: passing averages roughly +0.14 to +0.17 EPA/play versus +0.01 to +0.04 EPA/play rushing in neutral situations. Compounding over 15–20 neutral first downs per game, the cumulative EPA difference is material. The run game still serves play-action and short-yardage functions but should not default-dominate 1st-down scripting.
strategies.recommendation: On 1st-and-10 when the game is within one possession and it is not the 4th quarter, target a 62–65% pass rate rather than the league-average ~53–55%. This applies in any field zone beyond our own 15.
strategies.title: Pass-First on Neutral Early Downs

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=0.75 lies inside interval_95=[-1.2, 2.7]. Normal distribution has unbounded real support. No approximation; closed-form sigma derivation used.

distribution_family.justification: The defensive evidence is more mixed than the 4th-down or early-down passing literature; certain quarterback profiles (mobile QBs, quick-release specialists) may actually prefer coverage, and my roster's edge-rush talent interacts heavily with this effect, justifying a symmetric prior rather than right-skewing.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Multi-season EPA-against data show that defenses sending 5+ rushers on 3rd-and-long concede higher completion rates and more explosive passing plays (20+ yards) than four-man rushes with deep coverage. Sack rate increases with blitz but is outweighed by the cost of wide-open completions against single coverage. Limiting chunk plays is a stronger predictor of defensive win rate than maximizing sacks.
strategies.recommendation: On 3rd-and-7 or longer, drop 7 defenders into zone coverage (Cover-2, Cover-3, or quarters) and rush 4 rather than sending 5- or 6-man pressure packages. Reserve heavy blitzing for specific opponent tendencies identified in film study, not as a default on passing downs.
strategies.title: Reduce Blitz Rate on Obvious Passing Downs

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=0.30 lies inside interval_95=[-1.3, 1.8]. Student-t distribution is defined on all reals. Minor endpoint rounding: computed interval is [-1.25, 1.85] vs. stated [-1.3, 1.8]; discrepancy <0.1 points and visible in plot.

distribution_family.justification: With no analytical foundation and genuine two-sided uncertainty, heavy tails are warranted: there is a non-trivial chance this strategy misfires substantially (opponent scores on the very next series) or provides a larger boost than I expect (our defense resets and forces a turnover). Student-t with low degrees of freedom captures this tail risk.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu=5 chosen for clearly heavy tails (ν=4–6 range). mu = most_plausible_value = 0.30. t_{0.975, nu=5} = 2.571 (standard t-table). sigma = (high - low) / (2 * t_{0.975,5}) = (1.8 - (-1.3)) / (2 * 2.571) = 3.1 / 5.142 = 0.6029 ≈ 0.603. Check: mu ± 2.571*0.603 = 0.30 ± 1.550 = [-1.25, 1.85] ≈ [-1.3, 1.8] (small rounding at endpoints).

strategies.rationale: Analytics research on timeout value is almost exclusively focused on end-game clock management (the final 2 minutes) and covers timeouts as time-saving devices, not as momentum disruptors. My in-game observation over many seasons is that sustained drives accelerate once an offense reaches the red zone, partly because momentum within a drive is self-reinforcing for the QB's confidence and our defense's fatigue. Using a timeout to 'break the string' is a judgment call absent from public models—it is silent on within-game momentum effects. I flag this as a weak candidate: effect is plausibly near zero or even slightly negative if the opponent's offense uses the break better than our defense does.
strategies.recommendation: When the opponent has gained 3 or more consecutive first downs and crossed our 40-yard line, use a timeout before the next snap—even if it is the 2nd or 3rd quarter—to interrupt their play-calling rhythm, allow our defense to substitute, and reset the crowd dynamic on the road.
strategies.title: Tactical Timeout to Disrupt Opponent Momentum Mid-Drive

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=0.9 lies inside interval_95=[-1.3, 2.7]. skew_normal is defined on all reals. Parameters are numerically approximate; the plot script will display exact ppf-computed 95% bounds for visual comparison.

distribution_family.justification: I believe there is genuine upside (fatigue effects can be pronounced against top rushers), but also meaningful downside risk (hurried snaps increase offensive procedure penalties and can outpace our QB's processing speed), combined with deep uncertainty. Right skew reflects my belief the mechanism is real; heavy-like tails reflect the intuition-only basis.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically. For alpha=2.0: mode_z≈0.56. Mode≈xi+omega*mode_z=0.34+1.01*0.56≈0.906≈0.9. Standard skew_normal(alpha=2) has ppf(0.025)≈-1.60, ppf(0.975)≈2.37; scaled: ppf(0.025)≈0.34+1.01*(-1.60)≈-1.28 and ppf(0.975)≈0.34+1.01*2.37≈2.73. Stated interval [-1.3, 2.7] matches to within 0.1 points.

strategies.rationale: While hurry-up tempo and no-huddle offenses have received analytics coverage (pace EPA, two-minute drill efficiency), the specific targeting of individual DL fatigue based on consecutive-snap counts is absent from public research. Analytics models typically aggregate over full drives or quarters; they do not model within-drive exponential fatigue curves for individual linemen. My intuition, built from film review across multiple seasons, is that elite pass rushers lose 15–20% of their first-step explosiveness by their 4th–5th consecutive rush attempt without rest. This sub-snap fatigue targeting is qualitatively different from generic no-huddle strategy.
strategies.recommendation: In the 3rd quarter of road games, or following any defensive stand that kept the opposing DL on the field for 7+ consecutive snaps, deploy 4–6 rapid no-huddle snaps without substituting offensive skill players, deliberately denying the defense its normal rotation window and forcing their top pass rushers into a 4th–6th consecutive rep at full speed.
strategies.title: Concentrated No-Huddle Bursts Targeting DL Fatigue Windows

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value=0.55 lies inside interval_95=[-1.2, 2.0]. skew_normal is defined on all reals. Parameters are numerically approximate; computed bounds [-1.25, 1.95] vs. stated [-1.2, 2.0]; discrepancy <0.1 points and visible in plot.

distribution_family.justification: I lean slightly positive (fatigue is real and fresh legs help) but acknowledge the backfire risk: rotating too quickly disrupts gap assignment communication and stunts, possibly creating seams. Right skew reflects directional optimism; moderate tails reflect a reasonably bounded effect.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Fitted numerically. For alpha=1.5: delta=1.5/sqrt(3.25)≈0.832; mode_z≈0.50 (approximate). Mode≈xi+omega*mode_z=0.15+0.80*0.50=0.55. Standard skew_normal(alpha=1.5) has ppf(0.025)≈-1.75, ppf(0.975)≈2.25; scaled: ppf(0.025)≈0.15+0.80*(-1.75)=-1.25 and ppf(0.975)≈0.15+0.80*2.25=1.95. Stated interval [-1.2, 2.0] matches to within 0.1 points.

strategies.rationale: Public analytics tracks overall defensive line performance in aggregate but does not model per-consecutive-snap fatigue curves for individual defensive linemen. Pass-rush win-rate data exist in aggregate, but how those rates decay across consecutive reps without rest is not publicly modeled. My intuition, from tracking individual DL win rates on film over multiple game halves, is that freshness on a given snap matters more than continuity of rhythm—a fresher 6th-best DL on his 1st rep outperforms the starter on his 6th rep. This is a pure coaching-experience judgment with no public analytical backing.
strategies.recommendation: Rotate all four defensive linemen on a strict 2–3-snap cycle throughout the game rather than the conventional 5–6-snap cycle, keeping the full rotation fresh on every passing down regardless of score or game situation. Designate a 9-man DL group pre-game and cycle freely.
strategies.title: Hyper-Aggressive DL Rotation Every 2–3 Snaps
